Imagination cannot represent the grandeur such a spectacle might have displayed in the darkness of night. Hell itself would have supplied an appropriate comparison. Even in daylight my hair bristled as I peered far down into those gaping depths, allowing fancy to descend and roam through the strange vaulted chambers, glowing gulfs, and ghastly crimson chasms of that dreadful, bottomless fire. My escape had indeed been narrow. Had the balloon lingered only a little longer inside the cloud—had the discomfort of becoming wet not prompted me to cast away ballast—certain destruction must have followed. Such dangers, though seldom considered, may be the gravest that confront balloon travellers. By then, however, I had climbed too high for further anxiety on that account.

"My ascent was now rapid, and at seven o'clock the barometer showed an elevation of fully nine and a half miles. Breathing began to demand great effort. My head ached violently, and after noticing dampness on my cheeks for some time, I discovered that blood was flowing rather freely from my eardrums. My eyes also caused considerable distress. Passing a hand across them, I found that they appeared to bulge markedly from their sockets. Everything in the car, and the balloon itself, looked misshapen. These symptoms exceeded my expectations and alarmed me. At this point, thoughtlessly and with great imprudence, I tossed out three pieces of ballast weighing five pounds apiece. The resulting increase in speed carried me too suddenly, without gradual adjustment, into a layer of extremely rarefied air. The consequences nearly ended both the expedition and my life. A sudden spasm gripped me for over five minutes; even after it partly subsided, I could draw breath only in occasional gasps, while blood poured from my nose and ears and seeped slightly from my eyes. The pigeons seemed in dreadful distress and struggled to get free. The cat cried pitifully, her tongue hanging from her mouth, and staggered about the car as though poisoned. Too late I recognized the reckless folly of discarding the ballast, and my agitation became extreme. I expected nothing but death, and expected it within minutes.

Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, met Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay in combat. The four struck so powerfully that their spears shattered down to their hands. Then Sir Pertolope rode out from the castle to meet Sir Lionel. Pertolope, the Green Knight, knocked down Lionel, Sir Launcelot's brother. Noble heralds recorded all these encounters, noting who performed best and the knights' names. Next, Sir Bleobaris broke his spear against Sir Gareth, but the impact threw Bleobaris to the ground. Seeing this, Sir Galihodin challenged Gareth to defend himself, and Gareth knocked him down as well. Sir Galihud took up a spear to avenge his brother and received the same treatment. So did Sir Dinadan, his brother La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore le Disirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage: Gareth brought all of them down with a single spear. King Aswisance of Ireland watched these feats and wondered who this knight might be, appearing green on one pass and blue when he returned. Every time Gareth rode back and forth, his colour changed, preventing any king or knight from recognizing him with certainty. Then King Agwisance of Ireland charged Gareth, who struck him off his horse, saddle and all. King Carados of Scotland came next, and Gareth sent both horse and rider crashing down. He dealt the same way with King Uriens of Gore. Sir Bagdemagus then entered the field, and Gareth knocked him and his horse to the earth. Bagdemagus's son Meliganus broke a spear against Gareth with great strength and knightly skill. At this, the noble prince Sir Galahault called out, 'Knight of many colours, you have jousted well! Now prepare to face me.' Hearing him, Gareth took a great spear, and the two charged one another. The prince's spear broke, but Gareth struck the left side of his helmet with such force that he swayed back and forth. He would have fallen if his men had not caught him. 'Truly,' King Arthur said, 'that knight of many colours is an excellent knight.' He summoned Sir Launcelot and asked him to face the stranger. 'Sir,' Launcelot replied, 'I would rather leave him alone for now, because he has already worked hard enough today. When a good knight performs so well, another good knight should not rob him of his glory, especially after witnessing such tremendous effort. Perhaps he has a particular cause to defend here today. Perhaps this lady loves him above everyone else present. I can plainly see how hard he strives and pushes himself to accomplish great deeds. As far as I am concerned, therefore, the honour of this day belongs to him. Even if I had the power to take it away, I would not.'

"These were the circumstances that tormented Felix and made him, when I first observed him, the unhappiest member of his household. Poverty he could have borne; indeed, while he regarded it as virtue's reward, he took pride in it. But the Turk's thanklessness and the loss of his cherished Safie were sorrows more painful and beyond remedy. The Arabian's arrival now breathed fresh life into his spirit.

"When word came to Leghorn that Felix had lost his fortune and position, the merchant ordered his daughter to dismiss her lover from her thoughts and prepare to return to her own country. This command offended Safie's generous heart. She tried to reason with her father, but he angrily withdrew, repeating his despotic instructions.

"Several days later the Turk hurried into his daughter's room and announced that he had grounds to believe his hiding place in Leghorn was known, and that he would soon be surrendered to the French authorities. He had therefore engaged a ship for Constantinople and meant to sail within a few hours. His daughter was to remain with a trusted servant and follow when convenient, bringing the greater portion of his possessions, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

"Left by herself, Safie considered what course she ought to take in these urgent circumstances. Life in Turkey repelled her; both her faith and her inclinations opposed it. Some of her father's papers that came into her possession disclosed her lover's exile and the name of his present dwelling place. For a time she wavered, then finally resolved upon her course. Carrying her own jewels and a quantity of money, she left Italy for Germany with an attendant from Leghorn who understood the ordinary language of Turkey.

"They reached a town some twenty leagues from De Lacey's cottage without mishap, but there the attendant became dangerously ill. Safie cared for her with devoted tenderness, yet the unfortunate girl died. The Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the country's language and entirely inexperienced in the world's ways. Nevertheless, she found kind assistance. The Italian girl had named their destination, and after her death the woman whose house had lodged them made certain that Safie reached her lover's cottage safely."
